cue: How do you say it's wiser to let an enemy leave than to corner them?

es.text: A enemigo que huye, puente de plata
es.literal: to an enemy who flees, a bridge of silver
es.meaning: Let a retreating adversary go — smooth their exit instead of chasing them down.
es.example: Renunció él solo, así que no tuvimos que despedirlo: a enemigo que huye, puente de plata.
es.exampleTranslation: He quit on his own, so we never had to fire him — let a retreating enemy go.
es.regionNote: Attested in Spain (Siglo de Oro sources onward) and current in Mexico. Wider LatAm currency (ar, co) is plausible but unverified — reviewer to extend or trim the list.

it.text: A nemico che fugge, ponti d'oro
it.literal: to an enemy who flees, bridges of gold
it.meaning: Ease the withdrawal of an adversary who is already leaving; a cornered opponent fights harder.
it.example: Se vuole andarsene, lascialo andare: a nemico che fugge, ponti d'oro.
it.exampleTranslation: If he wants out, let him go — build the retreating enemy a golden bridge.

bridge.note: The same proverb on both sides of the Mediterranean, descended from the same Latin advice about leaving a fleeing enemy his road — and the only word that moved is the metal. Spanish plates the bridge in silver, Italian in gold. Underneath that, a quieter split: Spanish builds the enemy one bridge, Italian builds him several.

interference.es_to_it: The metal changes at the border. Italian pays in gold and in the plural — ponti d'oro. 'Ponte d'argento' will be understood and quietly filed as foreign.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish gives one bridge and it is silver: puente de plata, singular. 'Puente de oro' is not the proverb.

review.notes: Drafted by Claude 2026-07-25. SOURCES NOT HUMAN-VERIFIED — both were read out of search results, not opened by a person, so verifiedOn/verifiedBy stay null on both sides. Treccani carries the Italian under the `ponte` headword and in its guerra-e-usi-militari proverb cluster; the Spanish has a full CVC Refranero ficha tracing it to Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba with attestations back to Vallés 1549. QUESTIONS FOR REVIEWERS: (1) Register — both sides read formal to me, more newspaper column than conversation; if either is closer to `literary` or `dated`, say so, since formality is currently set ok_in_exam on both. (2) ES regions — is it live in AR/CO? (3) Is the plural obligatory in Italian, or does the singular 'ponte d'oro' also circulate? SCHEDULING NOTE: shares the ponte/puente headword with 0060 (hacer puente / fare il ponte) — keep them apart in the schedule, or run them deliberately as a pair. CROSS-REFERENCE: 0056 also has Italian reaching for gold where Spanish does not (il mattino ha l'oro in bocca); if a third turns up there may be an editorial thread worth naming.
